name: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
authors: Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, Denny Zhou; lead affiliation Google DeepMind (Jie Huang also UIUC). Huang and Chen contributed equally.
venue: ICLR 2024 (DBLP conf/iclr/0009CMZYSZ24); first posted as arXiv preprint 2310.01798
reflection_type: verbal-self-critique (analysis/critique of intrinsic verbal self-correction; the paper itself proposes no new method, it evaluates self-critique-via-prompting, multi-agent debate, and oracle-guided correction)
feedback_source: self-generated (intrinsic setting, no external feedback); contrasted against ground-truth-oracle feedback used by prior work (RCI, Reflexion) and against equivalent-cost self-consistency
iteration_structure: iterative-refine (multi-round prompting: round 1 = 3 calls, round 2 = 5 calls), evaluated against single-shot standard prompting; also evaluates multi-agent debate rounds vs self-consistency sampling at matched call budgets
reflection_object: output content / reasoning chain — the model is prompted to review its previous answer and reasoning and revise it; the paper studies revision of the generated reasoning/answer rather than prompts, skills, or weights
learning_locus: n/a (critique/analysis paper; no learning or weight update is introduced — it studies in-context prompt-based self-correction at inference time)
requires_training: none (no training; purely inference-time prompting study using GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, and Llama-2 off-the-shelf)
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge (intrinsic setting: the LLM acts as its own critic); the paper's central finding is that this self-judgment signal is unreliable for reasoning, and prior reported gains relied on a ground-truth oracle as the stopping/verification signal rather than the model's own judgment
distillation_target: none (no reusable artifact is produced or distilled; the work is an empirical critique, not a method that stores experience)
emergent_vs_engineered: engineered (the self-correction behaviors examined are prompt/scaffold-engineered, e.g. Reflexion/RCI/Self-Refine/Multi-Agent-Debate style prompting); the paper predates and is orthogonal to RL-emergent reflection in reasoning models
memory_type: none (no memory mechanism; single-conversation multi-turn prompting only)
memory_persistence: within-episode (correction occurs within a single task/conversation; no cross-episode experience retention)
error_localization_granularity: holistic/outcome-level (self-correction operates on the whole response/answer; the paper notes the model cannot reliably localize which reasoning step is wrong without an oracle, so correction is outcome-level)
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task (refinement is within a single task instance; no transfer of experience across tasks)
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: post-hoc-revision (model revises a completed answer after the fact); the finding is that this post-hoc revision frequently degrades rather than recovers correct answers
task_domains: math, QA/reasoning, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop QA, and (for the external-feedback / constrained-generation discussion) code and constrained text generation
benchmarks: GSM8K (1,319 test problems), CommonSenseQA (1,221 dev questions), HotpotQA (100-question closed-book set following Shinn et al. 2023); CommonGen-Hard used in the constrained-generation / prompt-design analysis (Section 5)
headline_result: Intrinsic self-correction degrades reasoning accuracy: GPT-3.5 GSM8K drops from 75.9 (standard) to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 collapses 75.8 -> 38.1; HotpotQA GPT-4 49.0 -> 43.0 by round 2. With oracle labels (Table 2) self-correction appears to help (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7) but the gain vanishes without the oracle.
baselines: Standard (single-pass) prompting; oracle-label-guided self-correction (reproducing RCI/Reflexion-style setups); multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2023) vs self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) at matched response budgets; Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023) baseline prompts vs an improved standard prompt on CommonGen-Hard
gains_vs_baseline: Negative/no gain in the honest intrinsic setting. GPT-4 GSM8K: -4.0 pts after round 1, -6.5 pts after round 2 vs standard prompting. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: about -37.7 pts after round 1. Llama-2 (Table 4) GSM8K 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5 and CommonSenseQA 64.0 -> 37.5 -> 36.5. Multi-agent debate (Table 7) 9 responses = 83.0 GSM8K vs self-consistency 9 responses = 88.2, so debate underperforms equal-cost self-consistency. Section 5: with a strong initial prompt (Standard Prompting (ours) 81.8 on CommonGen-Hard) Self-Refine drops it to 75.1.
compute_cost_profile: Self-correction multiplies inference calls: round 1 = 3 LLM calls, round 2 = 5 LLM calls vs 1 for standard prompting; multi-agent debate uses 6 (round 1) / 9 (round 2) responses vs 1 baseline. The paper argues fair evaluation must compare at equal inference cost, and at equal cost simple self-consistency beats debate. No training cost (inference-only study).
known_limitations: This is a critique paper documenting limitations of self-correction itself: (1) intrinsic self-correction without external feedback typically does not improve and often degrades reasoning accuracy; (2) prior positive results relied on oracle ground-truth labels as the stopping/verification signal; (3) multi-agent debate gains are really self-consistency gains and underperform equal-cost majority voting; (4) some Self-Refine gains stem from sub-optimal initial prompts that a single better prompt already fixes. Scope of the study: limited to a few benchmarks (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA) and reasoning tasks; the negative finding is specific to intrinsic, label-free reasoning self-correction, not to settings with valid external feedback (e.g. code execution / unit tests).
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: oracle-label/ground-truth — THIS is the paper's central thesis: reported self-correction gains in RCI (Kim et al. 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) depend on a ground-truth oracle label to decide when to stop/accept revisions; remove the oracle and the gains vanish. In the intrinsic-only (self-verify) setting performance does not improve and frequently deteriorates. The paper does endorse genuinely external/verifiable feedback (code executors/unit tests, e.g. Self-Debugging/CRITIC) as the case where self-correction legitimately helps.
self_correction_efficacy: net-negative for intrinsic reasoning self-correction (correction degrades accuracy across GSM8K/CommonSenseQA/HotpotQA on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2); requires-oracle to show net-positive gains. Self-correction is beneficial only when valid external feedback (e.g. code execution, unit tests) is available.
calibration_effect: degrades (paper's intuitive explanation: a well-aligned model with a good initial prompt already produces a near-optimal response; the extra self-correction/feedback prompt biases the model away from the optimal answer, so it tends to change correct answers to incorrect ones — an effect consistent with overconfidence/'reasoning tax'); calibration is not measured with a formal metric, the evidence is the accuracy-degradation pattern
failure_attribution_capability: classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy of evaluation pitfalls in prior self-correction work: oracle-label leakage; unfair-cost comparison vs self-consistency; sub-optimal initial-prompt design) rather than per-step or per-agent attribution
failure_mode_addressed: Exposes 'superficial self-reflection' / unreliable self-verification: the model cannot reliably tell whether its own reasoning is correct, so label-free self-revision flips correct answers to wrong ones (error introduction / over-correction). Also exposes evaluation failure modes: oracle-label leakage, inflated multi-agent-debate gains that are really self-consistency, and unfair-baseline (weak-initial-prompt) comparisons. Relates to MAST-style 'ineffective/superficial self-reflection' and incorrect verification modes.
builds_on: Self-correction methods it critically re-evaluates: RCI (Kim et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Multi-Agent Debate (Du et al. 2023; Liang et al. 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023); methodological references include self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022), chain-of-thought (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022), Self-Debugging (Chen et al. 2023b), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2023), and Constitutional AI / moral self-correction (Bai et al. 2022; Ganguli et al. 2023).
extended_by_or_inspired: Triggered a wave of follow-up analyses and methods on when/whether LLMs can self-correct, e.g. surveys such as Kamoi et al. (TACL 2024) 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs'; works distinguishing intrinsic vs external/verifiable feedback and small-model self-correction (e.g. SCoRe, Self-Rewarding/training-time self-correction); and the broader debate on test-time self-improvement for reasoning models. (Specific successor list approximate.)
on_policy_distillation_link: n/a / indirect — no distillation in this paper; however it motivates the on-policy-distillation / training-time line of work by showing that purely in-context (off-policy prompt) self-correction fails for reasoning, implying that genuine self-correction likely needs a trained signal (verifiable reward or learned critic) rather than zero-shot self-judgment.
sample_efficiency: Evaluated at up to 2 self-correction rounds (1 -> 3 -> 5 LLM calls); additional rounds do not recover and tend to further degrade accuracy, so more trials do not help in the intrinsic setting.
